claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a single-phase solid solution.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi solid solution is chemically random.
Single-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state lacks nanoscale chemical short-range order and associated lattice obstacles.
The absence of short-range order governs the low hardness and strength by permitting facile dislocation nucleation and propagation.
A suitable annealing and quenching treatment can induce nanoscale chemical ordering or clustering in the CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Short-range order can be induced in CoCrFeNiTi without forming secondary phases or changing the overall phase.
The random starting solid solution has uniform elemental distribution and only modest lattice distortion.
Annealing-induced short-range order creates local chemical inhomogeneity or enhanced lattice distortion.
The ordered or clustered regions act as dislocation-pinning sites.
Increased dislocation pinning raises resistance to plastic deformation.
Relative to the random starting state, an SRO-enriched annealed state will have higher yield strength and hardness.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on the degree of chemical ordering achieved.
The hypothesis is restricted to room-temperature, quasi-static testing of a single-solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi alloy without phase decomposition.
Failure to obtain both increased SRO and statistically significant strengthening would falsify the proposed SRO-controlled strengthening mechanism.
